hypothesis: Pointwise logloss training doesn't match the ranking metrics being scored (GAUC/nDCG@5 are computed per-user by comparing scores within one user's impressions); switching the FM's training objective to a pairwise BPR loss (sample a same-user positive/negative pair each step and push score(pos) > score(neg)) should better align optimization with the eval objective and improve primary score without touching capacity or features.

Per-user pairwise BPR (iter0) barely matched the pointwise baseline (0.6007 vs 0.6016 valid), likely because sampling just one random negative per positive throws away most of the ranking signal in users with many impressions. Switching to a listwise loss -- softmax cross-entropy computed jointly over all of a user's own training impressions per batch (ListNet-style: target = normalized labels, gradient = softmax(z) - target) -- uses the full within-user ranking signal every step and should align training more closely with GAUC/nDCG@5 than single-pair BPR.

Add a leave-one-out-smoothed 'user x author historical affinity' feature (bucketed long_view rate for this user with this specific author_id, computed from train-only counts, leave-one-out on train rows to avoid label leakage) as a 7th field. Unlike the already-tried coarse user-only bucketed features (which are constant across a user's own impressions and mathematically inert for within-user ranking), this feature varies across a user's impressions because the author differs per video, so it can directly reorder a user's candidate list -- giving the model a cheap, leakage-safe proxy for behavioral history without requiring a full DIN-style attention mechanism.

Diagnosis: pure listwise ListNet training (iter1) filters the per-epoch batches down to only users with BOTH a positive and a negative label in train, which silently discards a large chunk of training rows (users that happen to be all-positive or all-negative in train) that still carry useful signal for learning shared video_id/author_id embeddings -- this loss of data coverage likely explains why pure listwise underperformed plain pointwise logloss despite being 'more aligned' with the ranking metric. Fix: train with a HYBRID loss per batch -- a pointwise logloss gradient computed over ALL sampled users' rows (recovers full data coverage / global item calibration) blended (weight alpha) with the listwise softmax-CE gradient restricted to only the mixed-label users within that same batch (keeps the within-user ranking signal) -- expecting this to beat both the pure-pointwise baseline and the pure-listwise/BPR attempts by getting the best of both.

Replacing the fixed alpha=0.5 pointwise/listwise blend with a curriculum schedule (start pure pointwise alpha=0 for early epochs to let embeddings stabilize on the full population, then linearly ramp alpha up to a higher final value e.g. 0.7 over the next several epochs) should give the ranking-aligned listwise term more relative weight once embeddings are already sensible, avoiding the noisy-early-gradient problem of jumping straight into a 50/50 blend from random init.

Adding temperature scaling (T<1) to the listwise softmax cross-entropy term should sharpen the gradient's focus on the top-ranked candidates within each user's mixed group, better aligning the ranking-aware loss with nDCG@5 (a top-5-sensitive metric) instead of spreading gradient pressure uniformly across all of a user's candidates as plain softmax(T=1) does.

Replacing the ListNet-style softmax listwise term in the hybrid loss with a pairwise BPR term (sampling each mixed user's positives against a resampled negative, same curriculum alpha schedule as the current best) should better align training gradients with GAUC, since GAUC is fundamentally a pairwise-concordance metric and BPR directly optimizes pairwise score ordering rather than a full-group softmax distribution.

Replacing uniform random negative sampling in the BPR term with hard-negative sampling (draw a small pool of candidate negatives per positive from the same user, score them with the current model, and train against the highest-scoring/'hardest' negative in the pool) should produce sharper, more informative pairwise gradients than a randomly-chosen negative, directly improving GAUC's pairwise-concordance objective without changing anything else about the hybrid loss or curriculum schedule.

Averaging the BPR gradient over multiple (e.g. 4) randomly resampled negatives per positive, instead of just one, should reduce gradient variance in the pairwise term and give a smoother, lower-noise estimate of the true pairwise-concordance objective GAUC measures -- unlike the rejected hard-negative approach (which biased training toward specific hard negatives and hurt), this keeps sampling uniform/random but simply averages over more of them per update.

The current BPR term averages gradient contribution per pair, so users with many positive training rows dominate the update far more than users with few positives -- but GAUC weights every user equally (it's a per-user AUC average, not a per-row average). Reweighting each user's sampled BPR pairs by 1/(that user's pair count), then averaging over the number of mixed users in the batch rather than the number of pairs, should better align the training gradient with GAUC's actual per-user-equal weighting and improve validation primary.

Impression-level time-of-day (hour extracted from the log's 'hourmin' field) varies row-to-row within a user's own impression list (different candidates were served at different times), unlike the already-rejected coarse user-only bucket features, so it can plausibly help reorder a user's candidates and capture any time-of-day watching pattern (organizer direction #6, unexplored) -- adding it as one more categorical field should give a small positive or at-worst-neutral primary shift.
